summary: Mines 86,156 cumulative test-file patches from 33,596 agent-authored PRs (AIDev-pop, 2,807 repos with 100+ stars, five agents) and classifies each with a regex taxonomy of eight oracle-signal categories (five weak, three strong). Reports that most agent test patches carry weak or no explicit assertions and that, after covariate adjustment, PRs with multi-type strong oracles are more likely to be merged.

claims.claim: 80.2% of agent-authored test-file patches contain weak or no explicit oracle signals.
claims.evidence: §III-A/Fig. 1: 80.2% W1–W5, S1 11.3%, S3 5.7%. Regex classifier matched human labels on 86.7% of a 384-patch stratified sample; inter-rater kappa 0.77. But patches are diffs, so a modified file classified W1 may already contain assertions (acknowledged in §V); the headline mixes modified and new files.

claims.claim: On newly created test files, strong-oracle rates range from 18% (OpenAI Codex) to 67% (Claude Code).
claims.evidence: §III-A; chi-square 810.2 new vs modified and 2497.3 across agents, p<0.001. Cleanest measurement in the paper since the full file is the patch; no human-authored baseline to compare against.

claims.claim: After adjusting for agent, PR size, stars, task type and language, strong (S3) oracles raise merge likelihood (OR = 1.28, p<0.001).
claims.evidence: §III-B: raw merge rate is lower for S3 (59.7% vs 72.6%) but S3 PRs are 4.2x larger and in 3.8x more-starred repos; logistic regression gives OR 1.28. No regression table, no CIs, no model-fit diagnostics; observational, unobserved confounders (CI requirements, reviewers) acknowledged.

claims.claim: Oracle-aware CI checks that flag new test files lacking assertions would separate verified contributions from scaffolding.

patterns.note: Shows execution-based gates that count test files or green CI overestimate verification when agents write the tests; presence of tests is not evidence of an oracle.
Agent-authored tests bundled with feature work have strong oracles in only 18.2% of patches; test-first value depends on oracle quality, which agents often omit.
Proposes a syntactic/regex oracle check as a static gate on test diffs; not evaluated as a gate.
Field data from real GitHub PRs at scale rather than benchmarks.

methodology.sample: 86,156 cumulative test-file patches from 33,596 PRs in 2,807 repos (AIDev-pop, Dec 2024–Jul 2025); 384-patch stratified human-labelled sample
methodology.baselines: No human-authored PR baseline; comparisons are among oracle tiers and agents
methodology.models: Five agents: OpenAI Codex (65% of PRs), GitHub Copilot, Devin, Cursor, Claude Code
methodology.variance: Chi-square and Mann-Whitney tests with effect sizes; regression OR with p-value only, no CI
methodology.ablations: Sensitivity analysis reclassifying W4/W5 as strong moves weak rate <1 pp; within-agent, within-task, within-size stratification
methodology.languages: 30 extensions incl. Python, TS/JS, Go, Java, C#, Rust, Ruby; no per-language breakdown reported

standards.peer_review: Accepted at the 8th IEEE International Conference on Artificial Intelligence Testing (AITest) 2026
standards.artifacts: Replication package (scripts, classified dataset, figures) on figshare per ref [15]

biases.detail: Syntactic presence of an assertion is not oracle correctness (S1 only shows an equality check exists); merge rate is a weak proxy for verification value.
Diff-only classification inflates W1 for modified files whose existing assertions are not in the patch; only the new-file subset is clean.
AIDev-pop repos with 100+ stars; Codex dominates at 65% of PRs, skewing pooled rates.
Regression reported as single OR and p-value with no CI or coefficient table.
Without a human-authored test-patch comparison, '80.2% weak' cannot be attributed to agents specifically.

coi.affiliations: Danovo Energy Solutions (industry, non-AI vendor) and Kennesaw State University
coi.vendor_products_evaluated: Five commercial coding agents compared, none affiliated with authors
coi.detail: No author works for an evaluated agent vendor.

verdict_reason: Large-sample field study with a validated classifier (kappa 0.77, 86.7% agreement) and released artifacts; headline 80.2% is inflated by diff-only classification of modified files, there is no human baseline, and the merge-odds claim is observational with thin reporting.
applicability: For the Java team, a cheap deterministic harness gate follows directly: when an agent adds or edits a JUnit test in any of the repositories, require at least one value/exception assertion (assertEquals/assertThrows/AssertJ isEqualTo, not just assertNotNull or verify()) and flag mock-only tests, run host-agnostically in CI rather than per agent host. With spec-driven development, assertions should derive from spec acceptance criteria (schema fields, delivery API payloads), and verification should be a separately scoped task rather than bundled into feature PRs (18.2% strong for feature vs ~25% for bug/test tasks). Java is in the sample, but no Java-specific numbers are reported; 2607.18057 provides Java coverage data.

conflicts_with.detail: Same AIDev source; that paper measures coverage (Java 61.5% of changed lines covered by existing tests) rather than oracle strength. Coverage-based gates would look healthier than this paper's oracle view, which is consistent with its argument that coverage overstates verification.
